# Italy's hard right dissolves fascist past

By PETER SHADBOLT

ROME, Jan. 28 -- Italy's right-wing Saturday officially launched its party the National Alliance after it dissolved its core neo-fascist group the Italian Social Movement (MSI) in a bid to break with the specter of its fascist past. National Alliance leader Gianfranco Fini told the congress in Fiuggi in central Italy the birth of his party represented a reconciliation between the country's political forces. 'Today, the long, interminable post-war period ends in Italy,' Fini told delegates. 'If anyone had told us just a few months ago that representatives from parties far across the political spectrum from ours would be present at the congress of the political right, no one would have believed it. It is our miracle,' he said. Fini, 43, has long fought to establish his movement as a respectable and democratic right-wing party, independent of its neo-fascist roots. The National Alliance was created just last year from the core of the MSI, set up in 1946 by the followers of wartime fascist dictator Benito Mussolini. Delegates from the former communist Democratic Party of the Left received warm but muted applause from the right-wingers at the congress, but the most rapturous reception was reserved for vanquished premier Silvio Berlusconi. He told the congress the country must return to the ballot as soon as possible following his ousting and replacement with a technical, interim government. 'Together we must demand respect for the pledge to return to the ballot box in June -- together we must fight this battle and win it, God willing,' Berlusconi said. 

The National Alliance was one of the media tycoon-turned-politician's most fervent allies in the Freedom Alliance that won a surprise victory in elections last March. The Freedom Alliance collapsed and Berlusconi was toppled when his allies in the Northern League -- the second biggest party in the five- party coalition -- pulled out of the line-up. Berlusconi bitterly attacked Northern League leader Umberto Bossi at the congress, accusing him of betraying the pact and the electorate that voted the coalition to power. 'We were forced to give up (government) by a betrayal which will go down as one of the most wretched actions in the history of our republic, ' he said.
